evidence_set: HHE 1: during a traffic stop and vehicle search, a police officer in a short-sleeved uniform and without gloves opened an unlabelled rubber container outside the vehicle, and a gust of wind blew powder from it onto the officer, who reported powder all over the officer and the uniform; the officer tried to brush it off and cleaned hands and arms with hand sanitizer. Within 5 minutes the officer was disoriented and lightheaded, with blurry vision. The ambulance arrived about 10 minutes after onset; EMS staff washed the exposed skin with water and found the officer alert, with blood pressure 175/127 mmHg, breathing rate 17 a minute, heart rate 105 a minute and pupils of 4 mm, reactive; during transport the officer reported intermittent trouble thinking and staying awake. At the emergency department, about 42 minutes after onset, the officer was alert with no constricted pupils; during transport and the visit the heart rate was 80–85, the breathing rate 15–21 and the blood pressure 149/77 to 159/104; the officer reported mild blurry vision there, which resolved after several hours; no laboratory tests were done; the discharge assessment was chemical exposure. The forensic laboratory identified fentanyl and methamphetamine in the powder left in the container (1.56 g), and fentanyl in a compressed tan powder (9.98 g); the Figure 1 legend says material in a paper wrapper beside the container contained fentanyl. Editors' notes: the one incident on file in which powder later found to contain fentanyl reached an officer's uncovered skin, as the account implies (short sleeves, no gloves, hands and arms cleaned, exposed skin washed); no sampling of the officer's skin or uniform is reported and no laboratory test was done, only vital signs and pupils being recorded; the powder also reached the uniform outdoors in wind, so breathing it in or contact with the eyes, nose or mouth are not excluded (the authors consider all routes possible, PDF p. 6); the powder also contained methamphetamine, and raised blood pressure and heart rate are among the effects of stimulants the authors list (PDF p. 5); constricted pupils or slowed breathing, signs of opioid toxicity, were not recorded.

HHE 2: four officers developed symptoms while responding to a 911 call about an unconscious person with a possible overdose in a hotel room. Three entered, saw drug paraphernalia and powders scattered in plain view and heard the toilet flushed many times; they wore short sleeves, two wore gloves on entry and the third put gloves on shortly after, and they took turns to put on half-facepiece respirators with P-100 filters once powders were seen. One went back to headquarters to process a search warrant, using a computer and a camera used in the room; the fourth officer, who did not enter the room, helped there, handling the camera and other items from the room that had no visible contamination, and (Table 1) also cleaned gear and a vehicle at headquarters. Symptoms (lightheadedness or dizziness in all, with blurry vision, weakness, warmth, sweating, headache, numbness of both hands and the tongue, or feeling drunk, high or groggy) began about 25 to 90 minutes after the initial response for the three who entered, and about 30–45 minutes after first handling the equipment for the fourth (Table 1). One officer at the scene was helped out of the room, slumped against the wall and then to the ground, and improved rapidly after a colleague gave one dose of intranasal naloxone. Before transport all four were decontaminated (clothing and equipment removed, showered or washed with water, fresh clothing). None was reported to have depressed breathing; in the emergency department all had normal temperatures and were alert and oriented, none had documented constricted pupils, and the electrocardiograms were normal; blood pressure and heart rate were normal to raised, three had normal to raised breathing rates, and the fourth officer a rate ranging from 9 to 20 a minute; the officer given naloxone had no blood test, and the urine of all four was negative on a screen for cannabinoids, phencyclidine, cocaine, opiates, amphetamines, benzodiazepines and barbiturates; all were discharged after several hours. The emergency physicians' impressions were possible accidental overdose for the officer given naloxone and possible fentanyl exposure for the other three (Table 1). In the hotel room the laboratory identified dibutylone, N-ethylpentylone (2.87 g), heroin (0.14 g), para-fluoroisobutyryl fentanyl, cocaine, methamphetamine and fentanyl (0.14 g) (Table 2); the Results call these opioids, cocaine, methamphetamine and cathinones. Editors' notes: the opiate screen cannot detect fentanyl or its analogues, and most amphetamine screens do not readily detect synthetic cathinones (the article, PDF p. 7), so no officer had a test able to detect the fentanyl or the analogue found in the room, and whether the amphetamine screen used could detect the cathinones is not stated; when the urine was collected is not reported; no sampling of the air, of surfaces or of the officers' skin or clothing is reported.

The authors judge that the five officers' health effects were not consistent with severe (life-threatening or late-stage) opioid toxicity, whose signs include profound lethargy, shallow, slow or absent breathing, constricted pupils, slow heart rate and low body temperature; they write that low-dose opioid exposure may give milder symptoms along a continuum, that non-specific symptoms such as nausea and lightheadedness reported by the officers fit it, and that the improvement after naloxone in one officer suggests that opioids were a substantial component of a mixed exposure; low-level exposure to opioids combined with other drugs, particularly stimulants, might be consistent with the variety of effects, and adulterants or contaminants in illicit drugs might also lead to a variety of effects. The authors add that perceived risk might contribute to the observed effects: it has been associated with anxiety and symptom reporting apart from physical exposure, and its relationships with the exposures and the officers' clinical status were not assessed. Breathing in, absorption through mucous membranes, swallowing and absorption through the skin were all possible routes in both incidents; brief skin contact with fentanyl powder, or powder of an analogue, is not expected to cause toxic effects if visible contamination is promptly removed (citing three sources, among them the ACMT and AACT statement); alcohol-based hand sanitizer, as used in HHE 1, may increase absorption of fentanyl powder. Negative urine screens do not rule out exposure: opiate screens will not detect synthetic opioids such as fentanyl, synthetic cathinones are not readily detected by most amphetamine screens, the amphetamine and cocaine screens were negative at cut-offs of 500 ng/mL and 150 ng/mL, and results under a cut-off are reported as negative. Stated limitations: retrospective evaluations, interviews weeks to months after the incidents, review of the acute emergency department records only, so medical conditions not evaluated at the time could not be assessed afterwards, and toxicological data not always available. Editors' notes: nausea appears in no officer's reported symptoms in the Results or Table 1 (PDF pp. 3–4, 15); the reading of the naloxone response rests on one uncontrolled observation in an officer who had no blood test and whose urine screen could not detect fentanyl; no exposure was measured (no sampling of air, surfaces or skin) and no officer had a test able to detect fentanyl, so the article neither confirms nor excludes opioid poisoning in any officer.

evidence_set: An online pilot survey (SurveyMonkey), open from 1 February to 31 March 2019, written by the authors from a literature review and said to be validated for accuracy by experts in EMS, fire and law enforcement, with fifteen 6-point statements on risk perception (strongly disagree to strongly agree, with no middle option) and questions on knowledge and demographics. A flyer with the link and a QR code went to 15 associations of fire, police and emergency medical technicians in New York and nationally; 3 acknowledged and said they would distribute it; flyers were posted at the authors' universities, and first responders linked to those institutions shared it informally; agencies did not have to say whether they distributed it, so the overall study base cannot be ascertained. 247 responses were received; 187 came from responders serving New York State and no other state had more than 9, so only New York was analysed: law enforcement 92, EMS 55, fire and EMS dual role 25, fire 15 (Table 1). A majority of all disciplines had more than 15 years of experience, and 53.5% of EMS, law enforcement and fire/EMS personnel (fire-only responders are not named) had encountered fentanyl or suspected fentanyl at work. Editors' notes: a self-selected convenience sample with no knowable response rate; the other 60 responses (247 − 187) are described only as coming from states with 9 or fewer responses each; 53.5% fits 100 of 187, and also 92 of 172 (without the 15 fire-only responders), so its denominator is uncertain.

Information sources on fentanyl exposure and safety (all that apply): seminars or courses 78.1%, department training 76.5%, federal agencies 67.4%, professional or labor organizations 46.0%, social media or internet pages 23.0%, news media 13.9%; the authors read this as a sizable majority relying on official sources. The abstract says respondents generally agreed with expert risk perceptions, with lower agreement on hand sanitizer, glove type and skin exposure, and the Conclusions say those three items did not align with expert beliefs; the Conclusions add that the knowledge gaps reflect a need for better training through authoritative sources and a possible effect of overreliance on media reports of adverse effects from casual exposure. The Introduction says early warnings from law enforcement sources (reference 7, a DEA nationwide alert published in March 2015) may have heightened concerns, and that authoritative guidance rates the likelihood of an overdose from skin contact as very low (reference 8, a NIOSH video on preventing occupational exposure, published in March 2019; reference 9, the 2017 ACMT and AACT statement). The Discussion also states, citing reference 9, that harm from touching fentanyl is rather a chronic or long-term issue for people who touch it regularly or for long periods. Funding: none, apart from administrative support from the Christian Regenhard Center for Emergency Response Studies; no conflict-of-interest statement. Editors' notes: the sources question asked about fentanyl exposure and safety measures as a whole and is not linked to any answer, so the survey cannot show where the belief came from, and the suggestion about media reports rests on no analysis (13.9% named news media and 23.0% social media or internet pages); the 2017 statement contains no passage on chronic harm and says that no persistent effects are expected without prolonged lack of oxygen (Moss et al., 2017, PDF pp. 1, 4); the paper does not mention the DEA roll-call video.
